h: Why the haftarah of Adoniyahu belongs to this parashah

p: — The connection of the matter of Adoniyahu
הוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
— is according to what is written in the holy Zohar
— “a hundred, which is a great number,
,, — has ‘year’ (in the singular) written with it,” etc.
— that one should not grow proud
— of the matters of this world
— and least of all among the Patriarchs,
— that he did not choose greatness
— that he answered what they said to him,
, — “Let the world not lack its King,” etc.
— Rather, the main thing that needed teaching
— is that one not grow proud, God forbid,
— in levels of surpassing holiness and purity.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 122b (Chayei Sarah, Tosefta): "Whoever is small is great, and whoever is great is small, as it is written, 'And the life of Sarah was a hundred year and twenty year and seven years' (Genesis 23:1). A hundred, which is a great number, has 'year' written with it — He made it small; seven, which is a small number, He increased and made great, as it is written 'years'. Come and see: the Holy One, blessed be He, makes great only one who makes himself small, and makes small only one who makes himself great." This Tosefta is the frame of the whole maamar: Sarah's years teach that whoever makes himself small is made great, and Rav Tzadok reads the Adoniyahu haftarah as the counter-case. In the second quotation the print reads "whoever is small is only (rak), whoever is great"; read "…is great (rav), and whoever is great…", as in the Zohar. The print's misspelled abbreviation for "in the holy Zohar" is corrected as well.

h: Sarah's years: refined in all ten attributes

p: — And here, where it is written of Sarah
— it shows that she was refined
— and as stated in the holy Zohar
— that seven corresponds to the seven attributes,
— and a hundred to Keser Elyon,
— the most hidden of all hidden;
— and the number one hundred is a complete number,
— So too of Avraham it is written,
— “And Avraham was old, come into days”
— that is, into the first three (sefiros).
— And although earlier it is written,
— “And Avraham and Sarah were old, coming into days,”
— that they had been refined in all seven attributes,
— which are the seven days of Creation,
— and were coming to be refined
— in the attributes of the first three.
— This is because there was need
— for the soul of Yitzchak to be born,
— who was circumcised at eight days,
— so the parents had to be
— from the matters of this world.
— That is why Yitzchak was born to Avraham
— Therefore it is written “coming into days”:
— they had already come to be refined

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 122b–123a (Chayei Sarah): "A hundred years — the sum of all, all together, in the mystery of the hundred blessings of every day; and so too twenty years, which is included in the supernal one, the most hidden of all hidden (setima de-chol setimin). Therefore 'year' is written, the mystery of the unity that never separates... These seven years branch off and go out from the hidden sum above, and although all is one unity, they divide into judgment and mercy in many sides and paths, which is not so above; therefore with these seven 'years' is written, and not 'year'." The Zohar thus sets the hundred and the twenty in the undivided hidden realm above and the seven in the lower attributes; Rav Tzadok spells this out as seven for the seven lower attributes, twenty for Chochmah and Binah (ten each), and a hundred for Keser, "the most hidden of all hidden", the Idra's term for Atika/Keser.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 181a (Vayeshev): "When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, He made the moon and diminished her light, for she has nothing of her own (leis lah mi-garmah kelum); and because she made herself small she is illuminated by the sun and by the strength of the supernal lights." paragraphs.text: Zohar II 123b (Mishpatim): "And so we have learned in our Mishnah: the Hei was a Dalet; once the male joined with her she conceived one son and is called Hei; afterward she gave birth and brought forth the Vav, that son, who stands before her." The same formula appears in Sifra di-Tzeniuta, Zohar II 178b: "Hei was a Dalet at first; once she conceived the Vav within her, she gave birth." Malchus is a Dalet, "poor", until it receives from the nine above, and then it becomes a Hei; Rav Tzadok draws the moral that one becomes a chariot for Malchus only by receiving. "Be-seder ha-h" in the print is read as "be-seder ha-zeh" ("in this order"); an alternative reading is "be-seder ha-tes", "in the order of the nine".

"Be-seder ha-h" in the print is read as "be-seder ha-zeh" ("in this order"); an alternative reading is "be-seder ha-tes", "in the order of the nine".

h: David prays for his kingship only after the promise

p: וְכֵן מָצִינוּ בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
— So we find with King David, peace be upon him:
— after the prophet had promised him
— that You have brought me this far?”
— the word that You have spoken
— concerning Your servant and his house,
— That is: it had not entered his mind
— that it never depart from his house;
— only once the prophet had promised it
— did he “find his heart” to pray,
— to be a dwelling for the Shechinah;
— but of one who is proud
— it is written, “The haughty of eyes
— the Holy One, blessed is He, said,
— cannot dwell together in the world,”

paragraphs.text: II Shmuel 7:18, 25, 27: "Who am I… and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" (v. 18); "And now, Hashem God, the word that You spoke concerning Your servant and concerning his house, establish it forever, and do as You have spoken" (v. 25); "therefore Your servant has found his heart to pray" (v. 27). David prays for the dynasty only after the prophet's promise, which is the opposite of Adoniyahu's "I will be king". The print's "Hashem Elohai" ("Hashem my God") is given as in the verse ("Hashem Elohim").

h: Israel and the nations: greatness that makes one smaller

p: — And this is the difference between Israel and the nations,
, — ‘I am a worm and not a man,’” etc.
— for the greatness of this world
— the lowlier they became in their own eyes,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּנִמְרוֹד וּנְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר וְכַדּוֹמֶה
— Not so Nimrod, Nevuchadnetzar and their like,
— over what Hashem, may He be blessed, bestowed on them,

paragraphs.text: Chullin 89a: "I desire you, for even when I bestow greatness on you, you make yourselves small before Me. I gave greatness to Avraham…" The print's abbreviation "and Dav." is completed as "and David".

rich.text: : "I desire you, for even when I bestow greatness on you, you make yourselves small before Me. I gave greatness to Avraham…" The print's abbreviation "and Dav." is completed as "and David".

paragraphs.text: Parallels: (1) Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 42. Same Gemara and same move: the greatness meant is not this-worldly but "when Hashem bestows light"; from the revealed light "one can come to pride, God forbid, and then they would lose everything". (2) Pri Tzaddik, Vayikra 1: Avraham's worldly kingship "counted for nothing with him"; his "dust and ashes" came when his prayer prevailed, and Moshe's "what are we" is the higher level. (3) Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 7: after "dust and ashes" Avraham reached Atika, and after the tenth trial "ten times ten… in the supernal days". This joins the two halves of this maamar.

p: — that he was “exalting himself, saying, ‘I will be king’”:

— that is, he did not recognize

h: Why the Torah warns the king

p: — who merits to be a chariot for the attribute of Malchus,
— after he merits refinement in all the attributes,
— and then he would lose everything —
— is therefore warned in the Torah,
, — “that his heart not be lifted above his brothers.”
— that he has nothing of his own,
— and then he will be a chariot for the attribute of Malchus;
— he will lose everything, God forbid.

paragraphs.text: Devarim 17:20: "That his heart not be lifted above his brothers." Rav Tzadok's explanation is that the special warning to the king exists because a king who has been refined in every attribute is the one most able to grow proud. The print's "above those after him" (me-acharav) is corrected to "above his brothers" (me-echav) as in the verse.

— for this is the great cause for a person
— that he is born of woman,

— “What is one born of woman doing among us?”
— for this is the great disgrace
— and from this a person can
— and their names are hateful,” etc.
